Glances were exchanged, discomfort shifting in waves that slowly hardened into resolve. Not everyone agreed. But everyone understood. Whether from empathy or cold logic, they had found something to unify them: The Doctor’s toy had to go. Chapter 13 - Drift The Fog discarded him into halls that felt too cold, too wide. There was no grace to it. No fire, no roar. Just a soft thud of boots, and a man folding like paper onto the polished tile. Wesker didn’t get up. He breathed — at least, he thought he did. The air felt stale. Slow. He lay on his side, one arm bent beneath him, the other curled protectively around his midsection, trying to ward off the burning in his chest that refused to settle. Eventually, he blinked. Not because he meant to; more because his eyes burned too long without it. The Fog was gone. The lights overhead buzzed faintly. Somewhere, distant and high, a pipe ticked as if counting something down. He didn’t know how long he stayed there. — Time passed. Not in hours. Not in trials. Just... passed. Sometimes, his eyes opened. Sometimes they didn’t. There were stretches where he thought he’d moved, but when he looked again, the angle of the room hadn’t changed. Twice, he tried to sit up. The first time, his vision blacked. A red pulse knifed through his chest and flared at the cuff. It didn’t shock him. Just glowed. Like it was watching. The second time, he made it to his knees before something under his ribs spasmed so violently he bit his tongue hard enough to taste iron. He stayed down after that. The intercom crackled once. A long, thoughtful hum. A pen, somewhere, scratched paper. Then silence. — He lost track of how many resets came and went. Some part of him must have moved. Killed. Delivered. The body remembered the job, even if the rest of him didn’t fully. Somewhere in the blur between one gate and the next, he still lifted bodies, still heard hooks take weight, still felt the world approve in cold pulses against the inside of his skull. The memory of it didn’t hold; what little his mind managed to keep arrived as orphaned flashes, a hand slipping away from his grip, a generator flaring white in his vision, the sound of wood breaking as a pallet hit his shoulder. He came back from them more often with blood under his nails and grit on his teeth, and a cough that rattled deeper every time he woke — a pitiful little tell that he was still alive, a vague awareness that he had performed enough to be allowed to suffer again. A slow breath dragged through clenched teeth. Too shallow. His ribs didn’t like expanding much anymore. He tilted his head back to blink at the ceiling. He knew the angle of every light there. The layout of every vent. Once, this place had belonged to him. His stronghold. Now it just smelled like ozone and sterilized failure. The cuff at his wrist twitched; a light pressure, as if it wanted to remind him it still could. He didn’t flinch. Didn’t fight. Didn’t look at it. Just stayed there, watching nothing, until the pressure faded again. When he finally hauled himself upright, it wasn’t out of willpower. It was because the floor had stopped being safe. His pride, pathetic as it was, whispered that he couldn’t die there. Not like that. He gripped the wall and rose. His legs shook. Something in his left shoulder had seized completely. He didn’t bother checking the mirror. The last time he looked, he hadn’t liked what stared back. He didn’t know how long he’d been standing there. The room hadn’t changed. The weight hadn’t lifted. His arm had gone cold from the shoulder down to the cuff. That was new. The limiter at his neck had stopped burning for a while now. That should’ve been a victory, but he couldn’t bring himself to care. The cuff was quiet — simply because there was nothing left to punish. The overhead speaker clicked, the gentle scrape of a pen drifting through the halls. Shhhk. Pause. Shhhk. Wesker’s jaw tightened. Something behind his left eye twitched. A second click followed. Then a voice — smooth, clinical, and utterly amused. “Cycle 38. Subject upright. Minimal movement. Reduced reactivity. If I didn’t know better, I’d say we finally worked the tantrum out of you. Still holding, though. That’s my little soldier. You’re performing beautifully under observation.” The intercom snapped off again. He didn’t move. Didn’t growl. Didn’t scream. Didn’t answer. There was nothing left in his lungs to waste. Only a slow shift as he let his eyes close, a flicker of heat behind them betraying some lingering fragment of anger. But even that... Felt tired. Chapter 14 – The Break The survivors came back from the trials bandaged and quiet. Nea re-laced her hood with one hand, not looking at anyone. Claudette pressed gauze into the crook of an arm that had taken a bad wrench and said nothing. Jake rolled a shoulder that didn’t want to roll and wore his smirk like armor he refused to set down by the fire. Dwight’s glasses had a new scratch; he polished it without comment. They didn’t make speeches. They didn’t need to. Each return added a little more resolve to the air until the embers felt crowded with it. They didn’t get to plan fully. Not really. Not as a unit.
